NPM LIFECYCLE SCRIPT CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Did a dependency just start running code at install time?

Paste your package-lock.json and see every package that runs a preinstall, install, postinstall, or prepare script the moment npm install touches it. Add an older lockfile and this also names exactly which packages gained one since then -- the mechanism behind the ua-parser-js (2021), coa/rc (2021), and Shai-Hulud (2025) npm supply-chain attacks. npm audit checks versions against a CVE database and has nothing to say about this.

Nothing is uploaded. The text you paste is parsed in this browser and never leaves your device.

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file — and it can read your local node_modules directly, which gets the actual script text (a browser cannot read your filesystem, and a lockfile alone only records that a script exists, not what it does):

node cli.mjs snapshot --out baseline.json          # commit this once, after review
npm ci                                             # ...time passes, dependencies update...
node cli.mjs snapshot --out current.json
node cli.mjs diff baseline.json current.json       # exit 1 only if something newly gained a script
node cli.mjs lockfile package-lock.json            # or: just list what runs a script right now
node cli.mjs diff baseline.json current.json --ignore node-sass,esbuild

Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install. It reads only local files: no network call, ever.

Real, dated incidents that used exactly this mechanism

PackageDateScriptWhat happened

More: why npm audit doesn't catch this, and how to wire the CLI into CI. See also how this compares to Socket, an ongoing registry-aware scanning service, and why diffing package-lock.json by eye stops working once the lockfile runs past a few hundred packages.

Common questions

Why doesn't npm audit already catch this?

npm audit matches installed versions against a database of known CVEs. A newly added or modified install-time script has no CVE until someone reports it as one — by which point it has already run on every machine that installed it. This tool does not need a vulnerability database: it reports a factual difference in what a package declares it will execute.

Is this a malware scanner?

No. It reports which packages run a script at install time, and flags a small number of well-known attacker patterns in that script's text (piping a download into a shell, an obvious network call, obfuscated/encoded code) by keyword match. A flag means "read this one", not "this is malware" — a legitimate native-module build step can also match. It is not exhaustive and it is not a verdict.

Is my dependency data uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page parses the lockfile you paste entirely in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads only local files — no network call, ever.

What do I paste in?

Your project's own package-lock.json (npm 7+, lockfileVersion 2 or 3) — no extra step. For the diff, an older copy of the same file (from git history, a backup, or a previous run of node cli.mjs snapshot) goes in the optional second box.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It reports which packages declare an install-time script and flags a small set of keyword patterns in that script's text — it is not a malware scanner, not a security audit, and not a guarantee that an unflagged script is safe or a flagged one is dangerous. It does not replace reading the script yourself or a qualified security review. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The text you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also worth a pass over your dependency tree: License Drift Check diffs two snapshots of your dependency tree's declared licenses — the same "paste two snapshots, get a deterministic diff" shape as this tool, for a different supply-chain risk. And if your editor is part of your supply chain too: VS Code Extension Drift Check diffs two snapshots of your installed extensions for the same kind of newly-changed surface, the mechanism behind the GlassWorm and Nx Console incidents. And if a dependency name came from an AI assistant rather than your own memory: Slopsquatting Check flags a hallucinated or freshly squatted look-alike name before it resolves to a malicious package. And for a different publish-time question about the same dependency: npm Provenance Check reports whether a package was published via npm trusted publishing/provenance rather than a stealable classic token.

Free and open source. If this saved you some digging, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-diffing-package-lock-by-hand.html.text:
← Back to npm Lifecycle Script Check

This checker vs. diffing package-lock.json by hand

Every fact this tool reports is already in your own package-lock.json or node_modules -- hasInstallScript: true is a real field npm writes, and anyone with an editor and an older copy of the lockfile can grep for it and compare. This page names no product or company: keeping an old lockfile around and diffing it by eye is a manual habit, not a competing tool.

It genuinely works right after a dependency bump on a small project, checked by someone who remembers to do it. It gets harder to trust the moment the lockfile runs to hundreds of packages, the check has to happen on every merge rather than the one time you thought to look, and a flagged package's actual script still needs reading -- which is exactly what the table below covers.

CaseDiffing package-lock.json by handThis tool
A small project, checked right after a dependency bumpWorks fine -- a short lockfile is easy to hold in your head for one checkWorks the same way, instantly, with no need to remember to look
A lockfile with hundreds of packagesOne line flipping to hasInstallScript: true is not visually distinct from the thousands of lines around it in a diff-by-eyeParses every entry and reports exactly which name changed, every time, regardless of lockfile size
Knowing what a flagged script actually doespackage-lock.json only ever records the boolean -- reading the text means separately opening that package's package.json inside node_modulesnode cli.mjs snapshot reads the real script text from local node_modules directly, and classifies it against known attacker patterns
A lockfileVersion 1 fileHas no hasInstallScript field at all -- a grep that finds nothing can misread "field absent" as "nothing installs a script"Detects the missing packages map and says plainly that this format predates the field, instead of reporting a false all-clear
Re-checking on every dependency bump or Dependabot mergeManual, and the first step skipped once nothing looked obviously differentOne CLI command against the last committed snapshot; exits non-zero only when something newly gained a script, so it is safe to wire into CI

The gap that matters most: a boolean is not the script

package-lock.json's packages map records hasInstallScript as a single true/false per entry, because the lockfile stores the resolved dependency tree, not each package's own package.json contents. Spotting that a package now carries the flag tells you a script exists and nothing about what it does -- piping a download into a shell reads identically to a native addon compiling itself, until you open the actual file. A hand check that stops at the boolean has done half the job; this tool's snapshot command reads the script text straight from local node_modules and flags it against the same shell-pipe, network-call, and obfuscation patterns the incidents in this venture's README actually used.

The gap that matters second: the file nobody re-reads

A lockfile diff only catches a newly install-scripted package if someone actually opens the previous commit's copy and compares it, line by line, against the current one -- and a project with a few hundred dependencies renders that comparison unreadable by eye long before it becomes impossible. That is the exact window the four incidents in this venture's README used: none of them needed a victim to be careless, only for the routine "did anything change" check to not happen on that particular npm install. This tool's diff command does the same comparison in one pass and exits non-zero only when something newly gained a script, so it is the check that keeps happening after the novelty of a hand-check wears off.

When to still read the file yourself

This tool's risk tags -- pipes-a-download-to-a-shell, makes-a-network-call, obfuscated-or-encoded -- are a keyword match against patterns real attacks have used, not a verdict. A flagged script still deserves your own read: a legitimate installer can also fetch a prebuilt binary or a font file over HTTPS. What a hand check cannot do at scale is decide, every time, which of several hundred packages is worth that closer read in the first place -- this tool narrows that list for you; reading the flagged handful is still yours to do.

Common questions

Isn't hasInstallScript: true just a grep away?

Finding the field is a grep away. Knowing whether that is new since your last check is not -- grep on one lockfile has no memory of the previous one, so you still have to keep an older copy around and diff the two by eye. That is exactly the step this tool automates, and exactly the step most likely to be skipped after a routine dependency bump that shouldn't have changed anything.

How hard is it to spot one changed line in a real lockfile?

A mid-sized project's package-lock.json commonly runs several thousand lines across several hundred packages. The one line that flips from absent to hasInstallScript: true on a package you have never had reason to look at twice is not visually distinct from the thousands of lines around it -- there is no diff-by-eye reason it would catch your attention over a version bump on the same package.

If I do spot a new hasInstallScript: true, doesn't that tell me everything?

It tells you a script exists, never what it does -- lockfileVersion 2 and 3 record only the boolean, not the script text, because the lockfile stores the resolved tree rather than each package's own manifest contents. Reading the actual script means opening that one package's package.json inside node_modules by hand, which is a second, separate step the lockfile diff does not do for you.

What if my lockfile is lockfileVersion 1?

Then hasInstallScript is not in the file at all -- the field was added in npm 7's lockfileVersion 2. A hand check that greps for the field and finds nothing can misread "the field does not exist in this format" as "no package has an install script," which is the wrong conclusion for exactly the file where it is easiest to reach.

When does a manual look still matter?

Once this tool flags a package, reading its actual script text yourself is still the right next step -- a keyword match for a shell pipe, a network call, or obfuscated code means "read this one," not "this is malware." The tool narrows several hundred packages down to the handful that changed; deciding whether a specific flagged script is a real problem is still a human judgment.

← Back to the checker

No warranty. This is not a malware scanner or a security audit. It reports which packages declare an install-time script and flags a small set of keyword patterns in that script's text against known attacker mechanisms -- it cannot prove any specific script is safe or malicious, only report what it found. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. See the disclaimer on the checker itself for the full text.

Everything on the checker runs client-side; nothing is uploaded. Support is optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-socket.html.text:
← npm Lifecycle Script Check

This checker vs. Socket

Two different layers: Socket watches your dependency graph and the public registries on an ongoing basis for 70+ risk types, risky install scripts among them. This tool reads two point-in-time copies of your own package-lock.json (or your local node_modules), once, locally, and names exactly which packages run a lifecycle script and which ones gained one since your last check — no account, no registry calls, nothing installed.

What each product is for

Socket is a supply-chain security platform. Its own site describes deep package inspection that characterizes what a dependency actually does, rather than relying only on known-vulnerability databases, connected through a GitHub app, a CLI, and a browser extension. It flags more than 70 categories of risk across npm, PyPI, and other ecosystems — risky install scripts, typosquatting, malware, hidden or obfuscated code, and permission creep among them — and monitors changes to a project's dependency manifest on an ongoing basis. It is free for public, open-source use, and Socket's own site lists paid Team, Business, and Enterprise tiers for private-repository and organization use; today's specific prices and contract terms are not repeated here, since this session cannot verify them live against Socket's own site — only its well-documented product shape is described.

This tool does none of what Socket does. It has no account, no ongoing service, no GitHub app, and no connection of any kind to a package registry — it cannot tell you whether a name is actually published anywhere, let alone whether it behaves maliciously. It reads only what your own lockfile (or node_modules) already declares: which packages run a preinstall, install, postinstall, or prepare script, and — given an older snapshot — exactly which ones gained one since then, the mechanism behind the ua-parser-js (2021), coa/rc (2021), and Shai-Hulud (2025) npm supply-chain attacks. Paste the files you already have, or run the CLI against a checkout, and get every finding with its fix — free, in your browser or a zero-dependency script, with nothing uploaded and no network calls of its own.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want continuous, registry-aware scanning of my whole dependency graph for malware, typosquats, permission creep, and dozens of other supply-chain risks — not just install scripts.Socket — that is the ongoing, cross-ecosystem job it is built for.
I want to know right now, for free, which packages in this lockfile run a script at install time, and which ones are new since my last check.This tool — paste two lockfiles, get the diff, nothing installed.
I want a GitHub app or CLI that watches every future pull request for newly introduced risky dependencies.Socket — this tool has no memory between runs beyond the snapshot files you keep yourself.
I want zero network calls and nothing to install to check a package-lock.json or node_modules tree I already have.This tool — it never queries a registry, GitHub, or anywhere else.
I want to know whether a specific package has ever shown malicious behavior, or is a typosquat of a popular name.Socket — this tool makes no registry calls and cannot answer that.
I want a one-time, local diff of exactly what changed about install-time scripts between two snapshots, with the risky-pattern flags on each.This tool — that is the whole job, and the only one it does.

A team can reasonably run both: Socket for continuous, registry-aware defense against a live attack already under way, and this tool as a fast, zero-account, zero-network gate — in CI, at release time, or by hand — over exactly the install-script surface a lockfile diff already tells you the truth about. This page does not evaluate Socket's detection accuracy and makes no claim about it either way — it only describes Socket's documented product shape and states what this tool does differently. Socket catching a live malicious package and this tool flagging a newly gained lifecycle script are two different signals; neither replaces the other, and a clean result from either one is not a supply-chain security guarantee.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the check runs in your browser (or as a stdlib-only CLI script), and it keeps working with the network connection off.

Common questions

Does Socket already flag a newly gained install script the same way this tool does?

Not in the way this tool does. Socket's own site describes deep package inspection and real-time monitoring across more than 70 risk categories — including risky install scripts, typosquatting, hidden code, and permission creep — by watching your dependency graph against live registry data through a GitHub app, CLI, or browser extension. That is ongoing, registry-aware monitoring. This tool does the opposite and narrower thing: it never queries a registry or GitHub at all, and instead diffs two point-in-time copies of your own package-lock.json (or reads your local node_modules) to name exactly which packages declare a preinstall, install, postinstall, or prepare script, and which ones gained one since an older snapshot.

Should I use this tool or Socket?

They work at different layers, and a team can reasonably run both. Socket runs on an ongoing basis against your dependency graph and the public registries, watching for a live attack across dozens of package-behavior signals, as a service that is free for public open-source use and offers paid plans for private and organization use, per Socket's own site; connecting it needs a GitHub app, CLI, or browser extension. This tool answers one narrower, factual question with nothing to connect: did any package in this exact lockfile gain an install-time script since the last time I checked? Free, no account, no registry calls, works with the network off.

why-npm-audit-does-not-catch-a-malicious.text:
← Back to npm Lifecycle Script Check

Why npm audit doesn't catch a malicious install script

npm audit compares the versions in your lockfile against a database of known, reported vulnerabilities (CVEs and GitHub Security Advisories). That is exactly the right tool for "is there a known bug in this version" — and exactly the wrong shape for a lifecycle script, because a script has no CVE to look up until someone has already found it, reported it, and gotten it published. In every incident below, that gap was measured in hours to days, and the script had already run on whoever installed the package during that window.

Four times this actually happened

PackageDateScriptWhat happened
ua-parser-js2021-10-22preinstallnpm account hijacked; for about four hours, malicious versions installed an XMRig cryptominer and a Windows password-stealing trojan. ~8M weekly downloads.
coa & rc2021-11-04postinstallTwo unrelated packages (8.8M and 14.2M weekly downloads) hijacked the same day, carrying an identical malicious postinstall payload.
Shai-Hulud2025-09-15postinstallSelf-propagating worm: harvested npm/GitHub credentials, then republished a trojanized version of every package the stolen token could reach.
Shai-Hulud 2.02025-11preinstallSecond wave, moved to preinstall to run before scanners' own install-time checks. 700+ packages, 27,000+ malicious repos.

Each was a widely used or previously-trusted package, and in every case the compromise arrived as a change to the package's declared lifecycle scripts — not a new, obviously-suspicious dependency someone had to choose to add.

What --ignore-scripts trades away

npm's own --ignore-scripts flag disables every lifecycle script on install, which removes the risk outright. The cost: some packages genuinely need their install script to function — compiling a native addon, fetching a platform-specific prebuilt binary — so a blanket policy breaks them, and figuring out which packages are in that set by hand is exactly the tedious audit most teams skip. Knowing which packages have a script, and whether that just changed, is what makes a scoped --ignore-scripts or a manual review worth the friction on the packages that actually need it, instead of an all-or-nothing call.

Wiring it into CI as a gate

Commit a reviewed baseline snapshot once, then compare against it on every PR that touches the lockfile:

- name: Check for newly added install-time scripts
  run: |
    npm ci
    node ventures/npm-lifecycle-script-check/cli.mjs snapshot --out /tmp/current.json
    node ventures/npm-lifecycle-script-check/cli.mjs diff script-baseline.json /tmp/current.json

The command exits non-zero only when a package newly gained an install-time script since the baseline — a script that was already there, or one that disappeared, is reported but does not fail the build on its own. Accept a specific package's script with --ignore name once you've reviewed it, the same way license-drift-check handles an accepted relicense.

What a risk flag does and doesn't mean

Each script is checked against three keyword patterns — pipes a download to a shell (curl ... | sh), makes a network call, and obfuscated or encoded (base64, eval) — every one of them present in at least one incident above. A flag is a reason to read the script, not a verdict: a legitimate installer can fetch a prebuilt binary too. Only the CLI's snapshot command sees the actual script text; a pasted package-lock.json only records that a script exists, because the lockfile format itself doesn't carry lifecycle-script contents.

Common questions

Doesn't --ignore-scripts just solve this?

It removes the risk, at a cost: some packages (native addons that compile on install, some CLI tools that fetch a platform-specific binary) genuinely need their install script to work at all, so blanket --ignore-scripts breaks them. This tool answers a narrower, always-safe question first — which packages have one, and did that just change — so you can decide where --ignore-scripts or a manual review is worth the friction, instead of applying it everywhere or nowhere.

Does a risk flag mean a script is malicious?

No. The flags are a keyword match against patterns real attacks have used (piping a download into a shell, an obvious network call, obfuscated code) — not a determination. A legitimate installer can also download a prebuilt binary or a font file. A flag means read this one; it is not a verdict.

Why compare two lockfiles instead of just scanning packages against a malware database?

A malware database needs someone to have found and reported the specific malicious version first — by which point it already ran on everyone who installed it in between. Comparing what a package declares now against what it declared before needs no database and no delay: a previously-clean package that suddenly carries an install script is worth a look regardless of whether anyone has flagged that exact version yet.

No warranty. This page and the tool it documents report which packages declare an install-time script and flag a small set of keyword patterns in that script's text. Nothing here is a malware scanner, a security audit, or a guarantee about any specific package. Verify by reading the script yourself before relying on it. Back to the tool, or see how this compares to Socket.
